title: Multiple Linear Regression
abstract:
More than one input column. The best-fit line becomes a best-fit plane, and then
a hyperplane, but the algebra is unchanged — the normal equations solve any
number of features at once. This document covers the geometry, the full matrix
derivation, the crucial change in how a coefficient must be interpreted
("holding the others constant"), why standardised coefficients are needed to
compare importance, multicollinearity and its detection by VIF, and the
diagnostics that tell you whether the fitted model is trustworthy.

blocks.t: From a Line to a Hyperplane
From the notes

items: Input has more than one column.

Instead of a best-fit line, here it is a best-fit plane or
 hyperplane.

blocks.t: and for $n$ columns
\boxed{ y=\beta_0+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\beta_i x_i }
The goal is to find the lowest/optimal values of offset and slope.

blocks.cap:
One input gives a line in 2-D, two inputs a plane in 3-D, and $n$
 inputs a hyperplane in $(n+1)$-dimensional space. You cannot picture the third
 case — but the equation and its solution are identical.

blocks.t: Notation

$\beta_0$ is the intercept (the notes' $c$) and $\beta_i$ are the slopes (the
notes' $m$). The switch from $m,c$ to $\beta$ happens because with many features
you need subscripts, and $\beta$ is the standard statistical notation.
The Solution
The matrix form
Stack the data with a leading column of ones:

The column of ones is what makes $\beta_0$ fall out of the same machinery as the
slopes. Predictions are $\hat y = X\beta$ and the error is
E(\beta)=\|y-X\beta\|^2=(y-X\beta)^{ \top}(y-X\beta).
Differentiate and solve
Expand:
E(\beta)=y^{ \top}y-2\beta^{ \top}X^{ \top}y+\beta^{ \top}X^{ \top}X\beta .

Using $\dfrac{\partial}{\partial\beta}\left(\beta^{\!\top}a\right)=a$ and
$\dfrac{\partial}{\partial\beta}\left(\beta^{\!\top}A\beta\right)=2A\beta$ for
symmetric $A$:
\frac{\partial E}{\partial\beta}=-2X^{ \top}y+2X^{ \top}X\beta=0

One equation, any number of features. With $n=1$ it reduces exactly to the $m$
and $c$ of Topic 34.

The second derivative is $2X^{\!\top}X$, which is positive semi-definite, so the
stationary point is a minimum — and if $X$ has full column rank it is
positive definite and the minimum is unique.
Interpreting a Coefficient
The interpretation changes, and this is the main conceptual step

In simple regression, $m$ is "how much $y$ changes when $x$ increases by one".
In multiple regression,

\beta_j = \text{the change in } y \text{ for a one-unit increase in } x_j,
 holding every other feature constant.

That last clause is not decoration. It is why the simple and multiple
coefficients differ, sometimes dramatically.

blocks.cap:
Left: fitting each feature alone attributes the shared effect to both,
 so both coefficients are inflated. Fitting jointly recovers the true values.
 Right: as two predictors become more correlated, the estimated coefficient's
 variance explodes.

blocks.t: Simpson's paradox

The joint coefficient can have the opposite sign to the simple one. Ice
cream sales correlate positively with drownings; control for temperature and the
coefficient vanishes or reverses. This is why "which features are important" is
only answerable within a specified model, never for a feature in isolation.
Comparing importance requires standardisation

Raw coefficients are in units of $y$ per unit of $x_j$, so a coefficient of
$0.00003$ on income and $2.1$ on years of education are not comparable — the
scales differ by orders of magnitude. Standardise the features first
(Topic 13); the resulting standardised coefficients are in units of
standard deviations and can be ranked.
Multicollinearity
From the notes, and the reason Ridge exists

items: e.g. height and weight — two variables move together.

e.g. a duplicate: house area in sq.ft and the same house
 in sq.m.

a similar kind of multiple columns; one can be
 derived from the others — duplicates, essentially.

blocks.t: Why it destabilises the coefficients

If two columns are perfectly collinear, $X$ is rank-deficient, $X^{\!\top}X$ is
singular and $\hat\beta$ does not exist — infinitely many coefficient vectors
give identical predictions. Near-collinearity is the practical case: $X^{\!\top}X$
is invertible but badly conditioned, and

\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_j)=\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\left(1-R_j^{2}\right)\sum_i (x_{ij}-\bar x_j)^2}
 =\sigma^2 \cdot \frac{\text{VIF}_j}{\sum_i(x_{ij}-\bar x_j)^2},
where $R_j^2$ comes from regressing $x_j$ on all the other predictors and
\boxed{ \text{VIF}_j=\frac{1}{1-R_j^{2}} }

is the Variance Inflation Factor. At $R_j^2=0.9$, VIF $=10$ and the
coefficient's variance is ten times what it would be with independent predictors.

rows: No correlation with the other predictors

blocks.t: What multicollinearity does and does not break

items:
It does not hurt prediction. $\hat y$ is stable; $R^2$ is
 unaffected.

It does destroy interpretation. Coefficients swing wildly
 with small data changes, signs flip, and standard errors inflate so that
 genuinely important features appear insignificant.

blocks.t:
So: if you only need predictions, you can often ignore it. If anyone will read
the coefficients, you cannot.

Remedies: drop one of the pair; combine them (average, or PCA — Topic 33); or
use Ridge regression (Topic 41), which adds $\lambda I$ to
$X^{\!\top}X$ and makes it invertible by construction. The notes make this
connection explicitly: Elastic Net (Topic 43) works well when the input
columns have high multicollinearity.

What it catches

A single row driving the whole fit

blocks.t: Code

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, Ridge
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from scipy import stats

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
m = 600
exp = rng.uniform(0, 20, m)                 # years of experience
edu = rng.uniform(10, 20, m)                # years of education
age = 22 + exp + rng.normal(0, 1.5, m)      # nearly determined by experience!
sal = 3.0*exp + 5.0*edu + 20 + rng.normal(0, 6, m)   # true betas: 3.0 and 5.0

# =====================================================================
# 1. THE NORMAL EQUATIONS, FROM SCRATCH
# =====================================================================
X = np.c_[np.ones(m), exp, edu]             # the leading column of ones
beta = np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ sal)  # solve, do not invert
print("beta (intercept, exp, edu):", beta.round(4))
print("true:                       [20.0, 3.0, 5.0]")

sk = LinearRegression().fit(np.c_[exp, edu], sal)
print("sklearn:", np.r_[sk.intercept_, sk.coef_].round(4))

# The second derivative 2 X'X is positive definite -> unique minimum:
print("eigenvalues of X'X all > 0:", (np.linalg.eigvalsh(X.T @ X) > 0).all())

# =====================================================================
# 2. "HOLDING THE OTHERS CONSTANT" -- simple vs multiple coefficients
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'feature':10s} {'simple':>9s} {'multiple':>10s} {'true':>7s}")
for name, col, truth in [("exp", exp, 3.0), ("edu", edu, 5.0)]:
    simple = np.polyfit(col, sal, 1)[0]
    print(f"{name:10s} {simple:9.3f} {sk.coef_[['exp','edu'].index(name)]:10.3f} "
          f"{truth:7.1f}")
# Fitting one at a time attributes the shared variation to whichever
# feature you happened to include.

# =====================================================================
# 3. STANDARDISED COEFFICIENTS -- the only comparable ones
# =====================================================================
Xz = StandardScaler().fit_transform(np.c_[exp, edu])
bz = LinearRegression().fit(Xz, sal).coef_
print(f"\nraw coefficients:          {sk.coef_.round(3)}")
print(f"standardised coefficients: {bz.round(3)}  <- rank importance with THESE")
# beta_std_j = beta_j * sd(x_j) / sd(y) is the manual conversion:
print("manual conversion:", (sk.coef_ * np.c_[exp, edu].std(axis=0)).round(3))

# =====================================================================
# 4. MULTICOLLINEARITY -- age is nearly a copy of experience
# =====================================================================
def vif(Xdf: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.Series:
    out = {}
    for c in Xdf.columns:
        r2 = LinearRegression().fit(Xdf.drop(columns=c), Xdf[c]).score(
                 Xdf.drop(columns=c), Xdf[c])
        out[c] = np.inf if r2 >= 1 else 1 / (1 - r2)
    return pd.Series(out).sort_values(ascending=False)

D = pd.DataFrame({"exp": exp, "edu": edu, "age": age})
print("\nVIF:\n", vif(D).round(2))
print("corr(exp, age):", np.corrcoef(exp, age)[0, 1].round(4))

good = LinearRegression().fit(D[["exp", "edu"]], sal)
bad  = LinearRegression().fit(D[["exp", "edu", "age"]], sal)
print(f"\nwithout age: exp {good.coef_[0]:7.3f}  R2 {good.score(D[['exp','edu']], sal):.4f}")
print(f"with    age: exp {bad.coef_[0]:7.3f}  age {bad.coef_[2]:7.3f}  "
      f"R2 {bad.score(D[['exp','edu','age']], sal):.4f}")
# R2 is essentially unchanged -- PREDICTION is fine.
# But the exp coefficient has moved far from 3.0 and may even flip sign.

# INSTABILITY: refit on bootstrap samples and watch the coefficients swing
coefs_stable, coefs_collinear = [], []
for _ in range(200):
    idx = rng.integers(0, m, m)
    coefs_stable.append(LinearRegression().fit(D.iloc[idx][["exp","edu"]],
                                               sal[idx]).coef_[0])
    coefs_collinear.append(LinearRegression().fit(D.iloc[idx][["exp","edu","age"]],
                                                  sal[idx]).coef_[0])
print(f"\nbootstrap sd of the 'exp' coefficient:")
print(f"  without age {np.std(coefs_stable):.3f}")
print(f"  with    age {np.std(coefs_collinear):.3f}   <- far less stable")

# THE REMEDIES
print("\ndrop one:  ", LinearRegression().fit(D[["exp","edu"]], sal).coef_.round(3))
print("ridge:     ", Ridge(alpha=10).fit(D[["exp","edu","age"]], sal).coef_.round(3))
# Ridge adds lambda*I to X'X, making it well-conditioned by construction (T41).

# PERFECT collinearity -- the inverse simply does not exist
sqft = rng.uniform(500, 3000, m)
sqm  = sqft * 0.092903                        # an exact linear function
Xp = np.c_[np.ones(m), sqft, sqm]
print(f"\nrank of X {np.linalg.matrix_rank(Xp)} of {Xp.shape[1]} columns")
try:
    np.linalg.inv(Xp.T @ Xp)
except np.linalg.LinAlgError as e:
    print("X'X is singular:", e)
print("lstsq still returns AN answer (minimum-norm):",
      np.linalg.lstsq(Xp, sal, rcond=None)[0].round(4))
# Note it is A solution, not THE solution -- infinitely many fit identically.

# =====================================================================
# 5. STANDARD ERRORS, t AND p -- straight from (X'X)^-1
# =====================================================================
X2 = np.c_[np.ones(m), exp, edu]
b2 = np.linalg.solve(X2.T @ X2, X2.T @ sal)
resid = sal - X2 @ b2
dof = m - X2.shape[1]
sigma2 = resid @ resid / dof
se = np.sqrt(np.diag(sigma2 * np.linalg.inv(X2.T @ X2)))
tvals = b2 / se

print(f"\n{'':>10s} {'coef':>9s} {'std err':>9s} {'t':>8s} {'p':>10s}")
for nm, b_, s_, t_ in zip(["intercept", "exp", "edu"], b2, se, tvals):
    p_ = 2 * (1 - stats.t.cdf(abs(t_), dof))
    print(f"{nm:>10s} {b_:9.4f} {s_:9.4f} {t_:8.2f} {p_:10.2e}")

# =====================================================================
# 6. DIAGNOSTICS
# =====================================================================
fitted = X2 @ b2

# linearity / homoscedasticity
sl, _, _, pv, _ = stats.linregress(fitted, np.abs(resid))
print(f"\n|resid| vs fitted: slope {sl:+.4f} p={pv:.3f} "
      f"{'HETEROSCEDASTIC' if pv < .05 else 'constant variance, OK'}")

# normality of errors (needed for the p-values above, not for the estimates)
print(f"residual normality p = {stats.normaltest(resid)[1]:.3f}")

# influential points: leverage and Cook's distance
H = X2 @ np.linalg.inv(X2.T @ X2) @ X2.T
lev = np.diag(H)
cook = resid**2 / (X2.shape[1] * sigma2) * lev / (1 - lev)**2
print(f"high leverage rows (h > 2p/n): {(lev > 2*X2.shape[1]/m).sum()}")
print(f"influential rows (Cook's D > 4/n): {(cook > 4/m).sum()}")

# adjusted R2 -- the honest comparison across feature counts (Topic 35)
def adj_r2(y_, p_, k):
    r = r2_score(y_, p_)
    return 1 - (1 - r) * (len(y_) - 1) / (len(y_) - 1 - k)

for cols in [["exp"], ["exp", "edu"], ["exp", "edu", "age"]]:
    mm = LinearRegression().fit(D[cols], sal)
    print(f"{str(cols):28s} R2 {mm.score(D[cols], sal):.4f}  "
          f"adjR2 {adj_r2(sal, mm.predict(D[cols]), len(cols)):.4f}")
Worked Examples
Two-feature linear regression with the normal equation
Four rows, two features, target:

X = \begin{bmatrix}1&1
2&1
3&2
4&3\end{bmatrix}, \qquad y = \begin{bmatrix}4
5
8
9\end{bmatrix}
Add an intercept column of ones: $\tilde X = [\mathbf 1 \mid X]$, and solve $\hat\beta = (\tilde X^{\top}\tilde X)^{-1}\tilde X^{\top} y$.
Step 1 – the Gram matrix.

\tilde X^{\top}\tilde X = \begin{bmatrix}4&10&7
10&30&22
7&22&15\end{bmatrix}, \qquad \tilde X^{\top}y = \begin{bmatrix}26
 79
 56\end{bmatrix}
Step 2 – solve the $3\times 3$ system (Gaussian elimination gives):
Step 3 – predictions and error. Predictions are $[4,\;5.33,\;7.33,\;9.33]$, residuals $[0,\,-0.33,\,0.67,\,-0.33]$, so SSE $=0.667$.

Reading the coefficients. Holding $x_2$ fixed, one unit more of $x_1$ adds $1.33$ to the prediction. The coefficient is only meaningful relative to the scale of $x_1$; that is why features are scaled before reading coefficients as importance.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
Multiple linear regression has more than one input column, so
 the best fit is a plane or hyperplane rather than a line.

$y=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x_2$, and generally
 $y=\beta_0+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\beta_ix_i$. The goal is to find the
 optimal offset and slopes.

Adding a leading column of ones to $X$ lets one formula solve for
 everything: minimising $\|y-X\beta\|^2$ gives the normal equations
 $X^{\!\top}X\beta=X^{\!\top}y$ and
 $\hat\beta=(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}X^{\!\top}y$.

A coefficient now means "the change in $y$ per unit of $x_j$,
 holding the other features constant". Simple and multiple
 coefficients differ, and can even have opposite signs.

Raw coefficients are not comparable across features —
 standardise first to rank importance.

Correlation = two variables move together.
 Collinearity = a duplicate (sq.ft vs sq.m).
 Multicollinearity = one column derivable from the others.

Multicollinearity does not hurt prediction but destroys
 interpretation: coefficients become unstable and standard errors
 inflate. Detect with $\text{VIF}_j=1/(1-R_j^2)$; $>10$ is serious.

Perfect collinearity makes $X^{\!\top}X$ singular and $\hat\beta$
 non-existent. Remedies: drop, combine, or use Ridge
 (Topic 41).

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. How do you interpret a coefficient in multiple regression?

As the expected change in $y$ for a one-unit increase in that feature, with
every other feature held constant. That conditioning is what makes it differ
from the simple-regression coefficient, which absorbs the effects of everything
correlated with it.
Q. Two features are correlated at 0.95. Does it matter?

For prediction, barely — $\hat y$ and $R^2$ are stable. For interpretation, a
great deal: the coefficients become unstable, signs can flip between bootstrap
samples, and standard errors inflate so that genuinely important features look
insignificant. Detect with VIF and act only if the coefficients matter.
Q. What happens if two columns are perfectly collinear?

$X$ is rank-deficient, $X^{\!\top}X$ is singular, and there is no unique
solution — infinitely many coefficient vectors give identical predictions.
lstsq still returns the minimum-norm solution, which is a solution but not
the solution.
Q. Can you compare coefficient magnitudes to rank feature importance?

Not from raw coefficients — they carry the units of their features. Standardise
the features first, so the coefficients are in units of standard deviations. Even
then, importance is conditional on the model and on which other features are
present.
Q. Why does the intercept get its own column of ones?

So that $\beta_0$ is estimated by the same normal equations as every slope. It
also means the fitted plane is not forced through the origin, and it is what makes
the residuals sum to zero.

Q. Your model has $R^2=0.85$ but every coefficient is insignificant.
What is going on?

Classic multicollinearity. The features jointly explain the target well, but they
are so correlated that no individual coefficient can be pinned down — the
standard errors are inflated, so each $t$-statistic is small. Check VIF and either
drop, combine, or regularise.
